paragraphs: This paper models how a neural system can learn to move a simulated arm toward a target. Its motor command is distributed across several pattern generators rather than represented by a single output. For each target, the network chooses a subset of these generators and sets their activity, establishing the command that will drive the reach.

Learning uses signals produced by corrective movements. These corrections teach the network to generate a command that is largely prepared in advance, which the authors describe as quasi-feedforward. Sensory feedback still matters during execution: proprioceptive signals switch off the pattern generators. Each generator therefore has the task of recognizing when the arm has reached the target and stopping its contribution.

The simulations naturally produced a distributed command resembling population vectors observed in biological systems. The finding connects a movement-control task with a recognizable form of neural representation. Within this simulated kinematic arm, learning from corrections and using feedback to terminate activity were enough to produce that resemblance.
neurips-1991-a-cortico-cerebellar-model-.tldr: A simulated arm learns distributed reaching commands from corrective movements, with sensory feedback stopping the contributing pattern generators.

paragraphs: This paper presents a system that identifies which of four languages is being spoken in a high-quality recording. Its design divides the task between two neural networks. The first organizes the speech into seven broad phonetic categories, giving the system an intermediate description of the recording before it attempts to assign a language.

The system then computes phonetic and prosodic features from those categories. These features describe aspects of speech sounds and their delivery, and a second network uses them to perform language classification. The approach makes segmentation an explicit part of the recognition process: the final decision is based on features computed from the segmented speech.

Training and testing used different speakers of American English, Japanese, Mandarin Chinese, and Tamil. The system correctly classified 89.5% of test utterances. Separating speakers makes this result informative about recognizing language in voices outside the training set. The stated result concerns these four languages and high-quality speech, which define the application evaluated in the abstract.
neurips-1991-a-segment-based-automatic-l.tldr: A two-network system segments speech into broad sound categories and identifies four languages with 89.5% test accuracy.

paragraphs: Self-organizing feature maps arrange representations in an output space, making the choice of that space part of the modeling problem. This paper proposes a measure called the topographic product to guide that choice. It evaluates how well the mapping preserves neighborhood relationships: points that are neighbors should retain that relationship in the map.

The measure is intended to help optimize both the overall dimensionality of the output space and its dimensions along individual directions. These are related but distinct choices about how much room the map has to represent the data. Using neighborhood preservation provides a common criterion for evaluating them, connecting the map's geometry to the relationships it is meant to retain.

The authors test the method on synthetic mapping examples and speech data. For the speech application, it favors a three-dimensional output space, agreeing with recognition results obtained on the same dataset. That agreement supports the relevance of the proposed criterion in this application: its geometric assessment points toward a dimensionality also supported by recognition performance.
neurips-1991-a-topographic-product-for-t.tldr: A neighborhood-preservation measure guides the shape and dimensionality of self-organizing maps, favoring three dimensions for the tested speech data.

paragraphs: A probabilistic neural network represents each class using a sum of Gaussian components. In the standard version discussed here, these components are identical and isotropic, meaning their spread is the same in every direction. The paper identifies a weakness in this choice: changing the geometry of the feature space through an affine transformation can undermine classification performance.

The proposed Weighted Probabilistic Neural Network allows anisotropic Gaussian components. Their covariance can describe different spreads in different directions, giving the classifier more flexibility in how it measures the shape of a class. This directly addresses the restriction imposed by spherical components and makes the geometry of the probability model something that can be optimized.

The authors optimize the covariance with a genetic algorithm that uses a redundant logarithmic encoding and a large population. They report experiments supporting their claims. The contribution is a change to the probability model underlying classification: allowing directional structure gives the network a way to compensate for feature-space transformations that can cause trouble for the original formulation.
neurips-1991-a-weighted-probabilistic-ne.tldr: Weighted PNN learns direction-dependent Gaussian shapes to address the standard classifier's sensitivity to affine feature transformations.

paragraphs: This paper treats the structure of a learning system as something to choose dynamically. Its best-first model merging technique is intended to select a neural or related architecture while avoiding overfitting. The motivation is that an architecture fixed before seeing data may not reflect how much evidence is available or what structure that evidence supports.

The accompanying discussion emphasizes the value of individual experiences early in learning. When little is known about a domain, retaining an experience in detail can be useful because its important features are not yet clear. This perspective motivates a method that can change the organization of its model as learning proceeds, rather than limiting adaptation to parameters inside a predetermined structure.

The authors demonstrate the approach in selecting radial basis functions, choosing local affine models for curves and constraint surfaces, and organizing balltrees or bumptrees for efficient access. They report that it often generalizes substantially better than fixed structures. These applications show that structural adaptation can serve both predictive modeling and the organization of representations used during recognition.
neurips-1991-best-first-model-merging-fo.tldr: Best-first model merging adapts model structure during learning and recognition, often improving generalization over fixed architectures.

paragraphs: This paper examines how to estimate the local probabilities used within a hidden Markov model. Its starting point is a structural correspondence between radial basis function networks and tied mixture density models. Although these approaches can have matching mathematical forms, that correspondence alone does not make their learned behavior interchangeable.

The distinction comes from their training criteria: the quantities that learning tries to improve. The authors highlight how different objectives create differences between otherwise corresponding models. Their proposed method modifies connectionist training to resolve those differences, making the choice of learning objective central to how a neural formulation can support probability estimation in an HMM.

The paper discusses preliminary experiments with the modified approach and outstanding problems in discriminative training. Its contribution is therefore both a connection between model families and a proposal for making their training more compatible. The practical lesson is that matching a network's structure to a probability model is only part of the task; the training criterion also determines what the resulting outputs represent.
neurips-1991-connectionist-optimisation-.tldr: The paper connects radial basis networks with tied mixture HMMs and modifies training to reconcile differences caused by their objectives.

paragraphs: This paper translates logical proof search into energy minimization in a symmetric neural network. Given a first-order knowledge base, a query, and a bound on proof length, the construction produces a network that searches for a proof. The network belongs to the same broad style as Hopfield networks or Boltzmann machines.

The central guarantee concerns the network's global energy minima. If a resolution proof exists within the chosen length bound, those minima represent such proofs. This connects a symbolic requirement—having a valid proof—to a numerical objective that a network can minimize. The guarantee specifies what globally minimal states mean; it does not itself assert that every search trajectory reaches one.

The constructed network grows cubically with the proof-length bound and linearly with the size of the knowledge base. The authors place no restrictions on the types of first-order formulas represented and describe the network as fault tolerant and able to handle inconsistency and nonmonotonicity. The result provides a concrete representation of bounded logical reasoning within a neural energy framework.
neurips-1991-constructing-proofs-in-symm.tldr: A symmetric network encodes bounded first-order proof search so that global energy minima represent valid proofs when such proofs exist.

paragraphs: This study investigates what neuronal signals reveal about visual pattern recognition in monkeys performing a pattern-matching task. It focuses on neurons in inferior temporal cortex. The researchers use simple neural networks trained by backpropagation as tools for analyzing the relationship between the presented patterns, the behavioral situation, and the measured neural responses.

The analysis works in two directions. Some networks learn to distinguish stimulus conditions from recorded neuronal signals, testing which distinctions those signals carry. Other networks learn to predict the time-varying neuronal response from the spatial pattern of a stimulus. Together, these tasks examine both the information recoverable from neural activity and the relationship between visual structure and response waveforms.

The results indicate that the neurons carry temporally encoded information about currently visible patterns, remembered patterns, and behavioral context. The time course of a response therefore matters to its interpretation. The finding links visual processing with memory and task context in the measured signals, rather than treating the response solely as a description of the present image.
neurips-1991-decoding-of-neuronal-signal.tldr: Neural-network analyses indicate that inferior temporal responses encode current patterns, remembered patterns, and behavioral context over time.

paragraphs: Winner-take-all networks select the most highly activated unit from a group. The units are connected through inhibition, so their interactions implement a competition over which activity should prevail. This paper focuses on the behavior of that competitive process, especially whether the network settles into the intended selection.

The supplied abstract identifies sensitivity to connection weights as a major difficulty in conventional networks. Their convergence depends strongly on weight magnitudes, which must be adjusted by hand. Even after tuning, the inhibition generally works appropriately only across a relatively small range of starting conditions. A choice that works for one initial activity pattern may therefore be poorly suited to another.

The paper introduces dynamically adaptive winner-take-all networks in response to this tuning problem. The motivation is to make adaptation part of the competitive network's operation, addressing the dependence on manually chosen inhibition. The supplied abstract ends during that introduction, so it establishes the problem and proposed direction but does not support a specific account of the adaptation rule or its results.
neurips-1991-dynamically-adaptive-winner.tldr: The paper introduces adaptive winner-take-all networks to address conventional networks' sensitivity to hand-tuned inhibitory weights.

paragraphs: This paper studies how recurrent neural networks can learn a regular grammar from examples of strings that belong to it and strings that do not. The network must use the sequence of symbols to decide whether a complete string is acceptable. The authors use simple second-order recurrent networks and demonstrate learning and rule extraction for deterministic regular grammars.

Training uses an incremental form of real-time recurrent learning. It computes the complete gradient and updates the network's weights at the end of each string. During or after training, a dynamic clustering procedure extracts the production rules learned by the network, turning its learned behavior into an explicit grammar.

In many of the reported cases, the extracted grammar classifies unseen strings more accurately than the network from which it came. Rule extraction therefore serves more than an explanatory purpose: it can improve the usable result of learning. The approach connects learning from labeled examples with recovering a symbolic description that can itself recognize new strings.
neurips-1991-extracting-and-learning-an-.tldr: Recurrent networks learn regular grammars from labeled strings, and extracted symbolic grammars often classify unseen strings better than their source networks.

paragraphs: This paper presents a neural architecture for finding two-dimensional shapes within complex images when their positions and sizes are unknown. The task is localization: identifying where relevant shapes appear in a scene. To accommodate different object sizes, the authors build scale variation into the network itself.

The application is locating the identification-number characters on railroad cars in video images. This setting includes substantial changes in illumination and characters that are often visually poor. Searching across scale is relevant because the system cannot begin with an assumed character size, just as it cannot begin with the characters' positions already supplied.

In a database of 300 images, the method correctly located more than 95% of the characters. That figure describes successful localization, rather than a stated rate for recognizing the characters' identities. The implementation also combines computing platforms: part of the network runs on a processor board containing an analog neural chip, while the remainder runs as software on a workstation or digital signal processor.
neurips-1991-image-segmentation-with-net.tldr: A neural network with built-in scale variation located over 95% of railroad-car identification characters across 300 images.

paragraphs: This paper combines hidden Markov models with radial basis function networks to recognize isolated spoken words from different speakers. The division of labor is deliberate: the neural network supplies static pattern classification, while HMM decoding handles the temporal alignment needed to interpret speech as a sequence.

Radial basis function networks were chosen because they offered classification performance comparable to other networks and could be trained rapidly through a one-pass matrix inversion method. On a speaker-independent E-set database, the hybrid system achieved an error rate of 11.5%, compared with 15.7% for the unimodal Gaussian HMM system on which it was based.

Additional experiments suggest that radial basis networks may achieve good performance with fewer parameters than Gaussian mixture classifiers. The paper also reports an unsuccessful extension: global parameter optimization aimed directly at overall word error did not reduce the error rate. The evidence therefore supports the hybrid architecture's improvement in this evaluation while separating that success from the attempted change in optimization objective.
neurips-1991-improved-hidden-markov-mode.tldr: An HMM–radial basis network hybrid reduced isolated-word recognition error from 15.7% to 11.5% in the reported speaker-independent evaluation.

paragraphs: This paper asks how to select a small amount of data that still permits a good reconstruction of a larger surface. It frames learning an input-output mapping as surface reconstruction, where the retained observations must preserve enough structure for an approximate reconstruction. Images are one example of the piecewise smooth surfaces considered.

The authors connect this selection problem to both information compression by removing data and learning how to teach. A useful teacher chooses examples according to what a model can reconstruct from them. Their key step is a statistical selection process guided by the model, with the system able to predict the approximated surface produced by the selected observations.

For piecewise smooth surfaces, the authors use mean field techniques to obtain a deterministic network and demonstrate image-data compression. The contribution makes example selection depend on the reconstruction it enables. This gives the retained data a clear purpose: each selection is evaluated through the surface that can be learned from the reduced information.
neurips-1991-learning-how-to-teach-or-se.tldr: A model-guided selection process compresses surface data by choosing sparse examples that support an approximate reconstruction.

paragraphs: Vestibular compensation is the recovery of normal functioning after one of the paired peripheral vestibular receptors is destroyed. This paper studies that recovery through a dynamic neural network model of the vestibulo-ocular reflex. The researchers lesion the model and then retrain it with recurrent backpropagation, treating compensation as a learning process.

The retrained model reproduces the neuronal activity pattern observed experimentally in compensated animals, but only under a particular condition. Connections previously regarded as uninvolved must be allowed to change. Within the model, the ability to adapt those connections is necessary to match the observed recovery pattern, making their possible role a central finding.

The network also uses nonlinear units, which allow it to reconcile previously conflicting linear analyses of neuronal dynamics in normal and compensated animals. The modeling result links the interpretation of recovery to both connection plasticity and nonlinear response behavior. It offers a computational account of how these features can jointly explain activity patterns associated with compensation.
neurips-1991-learning-in-the-vestibular-.tldr: A recurrent model reproduces vestibular compensation only when previously discounted connections can adapt, while nonlinear units reconcile conflicting analyses.

paragraphs: This paper proposes compressing sequence history by learning what can already be predicted. A network first learns to predict its next input from previous inputs. Predictable events need not be passed upward individually; unexpected inputs, together with their occurrence times, become the input to a higher-level predictor.

Repeating this process builds a hierarchy whose higher levels operate on slower, self-adjusting timescales. Each level focuses on events that the level below could not predict. The authors describe the resulting sequence representations as reduced without loss of information, with timing retained as part of the description. These representations are intended to make supervised or reinforcement learning easier.

The paper also describes using two recurrent networks to collapse a predictor hierarchy into a single recurrent network, and extending predictability from a binary decision to a continuous quantity. Experiments show that systems based on these principles can need less computation per step and many fewer training sequences than conventional recurrent-network training. The contribution is a way of organizing sequence information that can work with different learning algorithms.
neurips-1991-learning-unambiguous-reduce.tldr: A hierarchy of predictors compresses sequences by passing unexpected events and their timing upward, reducing learning and computational demands in experiments.

paragraphs: This paper addresses recognizing a three-dimensional object when its image changes with viewpoint. It represents each view as a collection of points specified by their positions in the image. An object model contains several two-dimensional views together with correspondences indicating which points match across those views.

The central result is that a novel view can be expressed as a linear combination of the stored views within this representation. That makes the relationships among views usable through linear operations. The point correspondences are an explicit part of the model: the stored images provide coordinated descriptions of the same object's points across viewpoints.

Using this result, the authors construct a linear operator that distinguishes views of a particular object from views of other objects. They also show that relatively simple neural architectures can implement the operator. The contribution connects viewpoint-dependent recognition to a compact mathematical operation, with the representation of corresponding image points providing the basis for recognizing previously unstored views.
neurips-1991-linear-operator-for-object-.tldr: Corresponding points across stored object views support a linear operator for recognizing novel views of that object.

paragraphs: This paper applies neural networks to satellite remote sensing observations. The authors describe an application whose complexity and data volume make a single method insufficient. Their proposed response is a multimodule architecture in which several neural networks cooperate, making the organization of the overall system part of the solution.

The work addresses generic problems that arise when combining multiple neural modules. The resulting system supports both multivalued function approximation and probability estimation. These capabilities matter because the architecture must do more than produce one simple prediction: it must accommodate the different forms of modeling required by the remote sensing application.

The authors report accurate performance and compare their results with six other methods previously used for the problem. They also argue that the methodology extends to a broad range of applications. The contribution is therefore a cooperative modeling strategy, illustrated through remote sensing, in which solutions to shared architectural problems help several networks function together as a useful estimation system.
neurips-1991-multimodular-architecture-f.tldr: A cooperative architecture of neural modules tackles complex satellite remote sensing tasks involving function approximation and probability estimation.

paragraphs: This paper studies how activity across a neural network can alter the operating properties of an individual neuron. It focuses on input resistance and the time and space constants that influence excitability and the integration of signals. These properties determine how a cell combines inputs arriving at different locations and times.

The authors use detailed computer simulations of neocortical pyramidal cells. Their simulations show that spontaneous background firing can set these cellular parameters. The mechanism is a substantial change in membrane conductance caused by synaptic activity, involving excitatory and inhibitory inputs and the excitatory receptor types described in the abstract.

The result makes the surrounding network's activity part of the explanation for a single cell's behavior. A neuron's integration properties are not treated as fixed ingredients supplied to the network; they can depend on the network's ongoing activity. This matters for interpreting cellular responses because the background state helps determine how subsequent signals are combined and how readily the cell responds.
neurips-1991-network-activity-determines.tldr: Simulations show that spontaneous network activity changes membrane conductance and thereby controls how individual neurons integrate inputs.

paragraphs: This paper investigates a theoretical tradeoff between network depth and the magnitude of connection weights. Its networks consist of linear threshold elements, which make decisions from weighted inputs. The concern is that weights can become prohibitively large as input size grows, even when the number of network elements remains manageable.

The main theorem shows how to replace large integer weights with smaller ones by increasing depth. Every polynomial-size network of depth d with exponentially large integer weights can be simulated by a polynomial-size network of depth 2d + 1 whose integer weights are polynomially bounded. The replacement preserves the computation while changing the resources used to express it.

The proof uses harmonic analysis of Boolean functions. The same technique also improves known depth results for threshold networks computing comparison, addition, and multiplication of two binary numbers, as well as maximum and sorting over multiple numbers. The contribution shows that large weight magnitudes are not always essential: additional layers can provide an efficient alternative in this formal network setting.
neurips-1991-neural-computing-with-small.tldr: Threshold networks with exponentially large weights can be simulated using polynomially bounded weights by increasing depth from d to 2d + 1.

paragraphs: This paper makes neural-network architecture selection depend on prediction risk: expected performance on new observations. The authors use this quantity as a precise definition of generalization ability and choose among candidate multilayer perceptron architectures according to estimated risk. The aim is to select a structure for its predictive usefulness beyond the available examples.

Because prediction risk is not directly known, the method estimates it from data. The paper considers v-fold cross-validation and asymptotic approximations based on generalized cross-validation or Akaike's final prediction error. It also proposes a heuristic search strategy for exploring possible architectures, connecting the evaluation criterion with a way to navigate the choices.

The application is corporate bond rating prediction, where data are limited and a complete prior model is unavailable to dictate network structure. Those conditions make architecture selection especially consequential. The contribution is a procedure that uses estimated generalization performance to guide the choice, bringing both the search process and the assessment of candidate networks into an explicit statistical framework.
neurips-1991-principled-architecture-sel.tldr: The paper selects neural architectures using estimated prediction risk and applies the approach to corporate bond rating prediction with limited data.

paragraphs: This paper develops MANNCON, an algorithm that turns the equations of a PID controller into a neural network's topology and initial weights. The network then undergoes further training through backpropagation. Existing controller knowledge therefore supplies a concrete starting structure and behavior that learning can refine.

The approach extends the idea behind KBANN, which uses networks to refine knowledge expressed as simple propositional rules. Here the starting knowledge is mathematical control equations. Encoding those equations into the network connects an established controller design with a trainable representation, allowing the initial control policy to shape both the network's organization and its starting parameters.

The authors apply the method to controlling water-tank outflow and temperature. They report statistically significant accuracy gains over both a standard neural-network approach and a PID controller that does not learn. They also find significantly less variation in test accuracy when weights are initialized from PID knowledge rather than small random values. In this application, informed initialization improves both accuracy and consistency.
neurips-1991-refining-pid-controllers-us.tldr: Initializing a trainable network from PID equations improves water-tank control accuracy and reduces variation in test performance.

paragraphs: This paper studies a training schedule that repeatedly presents the same example until its error falls to a chosen criterion. Only then does the system randomly select another example. The decision about when to move on is therefore tied to the learner's current performance on the item being practiced.

This changes the usual arrangement in which each example is selected independently from a fixed distribution. Under the proposed schedule, a selected item can occupy several successive training presentations. The error criterion controls when that repetition ends, making it a central part of the learning procedure rather than merely a way of reporting progress.

The analysis finds that the strategy can dramatically shorten or lengthen convergence time, depending on the task. Its effect is also highly sensitive to the selected criterion. Repetition is therefore a consequential training choice whose benefit depends on how it is configured. The paper's finding draws attention to example scheduling as a factor that can substantially change learning speed.
neurips-1991-repeat-until-bored-a-patter.tldr: Repeating an example until its error meets a threshold can greatly speed up or slow down learning, depending on the task and threshold.

paragraphs: This paper compares two goals for training a classifier. The probabilistic strategy learns the posterior probability of every class. The differential strategy focuses on identifying the class with the largest posterior probability, because that identity determines the optimal classification decision. The distinction concerns how much information the learner must recover to make a decision.

The authors connect each strategy to a family of training objectives. Probabilistic learning includes mean-squared error and cross-entropy, while differential learning uses classification figure-of-merit objectives. They prove that learning posterior distributions requires larger training sets and more complex classifiers than approximating the Bayesian decision function itself. Their differential strategy achieves the stated minimum requirements for a specified error-based precision.

The proofs use repeated throws of an unfair die with multiple sides. This game provides a way to separate estimating all outcome probabilities from determining which outcome is most likely. The authors extend that reasoning into an information-theoretic model of sample complexity for statistical pattern recognition, linking the information demanded by an objective to the resources needed to learn it.
neurips-1991-shooting-craps-in-search-of.tldr: The paper proves resource advantages for learning the optimal class decision directly instead of estimating every class's posterior probability.

paragraphs: This paper asks which kinds of target functions are well suited to particular network architectures. It studies projection pursuit learning networks, whose structure closely resembles a neural network with one sigmoidal hidden layer. The focus is approximation: how the form of a network interacts with the mathematical properties of the function it is meant to represent.

The authors develop a general method based on a continuous version of projection pursuit regression. Their analysis shows better approximation behavior for angular smooth functions than for Laplacian smooth functions. These are different mathematical notions of smoothness, so the finding makes the type of regularity in the target function relevant to architecture choice.

The paper also establishes the existence of a ridge-function approximation scheme that avoids the curse of dimensionality in the stated L2 setting. Together, these results connect approximation difficulty with both function structure and representation. The contribution gives theoretical reasons to consider how a problem's smoothness aligns with projection-based representations when evaluating whether that architecture is suitable.
neurips-1991-some-approximation-properti.tldr: The paper links projection pursuit approximation quality to function smoothness and establishes a ridge-function scheme that avoids dimensionality's usual burden.

paragraphs: This paper studies harmoniums, a type of Boltzmann machine with a bipartite structure, as models of probability distributions over binary input vectors. The first question is representational capacity. The authors show that, for any fixed positive input dimension, these machines can approximate any distribution over the possible binary vectors arbitrarily closely.

The paper then presents two learning methods. The first uses gradient ascent to seek maximum-likelihood parameter estimates. For this network structure, the authors derive a closed-form gradient that is substantially easier to compute than the corresponding gradient for a general Boltzmann machine. The structural restriction therefore provides a useful simplification while retaining broad representational capacity.

The second method constructs the model greedily, creating hidden units and determining their weights one at a time. It adapts an approach from projection pursuit density estimation. Experiments examine both learning methods on synthetic data and handwritten-digit data. The contribution combines an expressiveness result with two concrete routes for fitting the model: adjusting its parameters jointly or building hidden structure incrementally.
neurips-1991-unsupervised-learning-of-di.tldr: Two-layer harmoniums can approximate any binary-vector distribution, and the paper develops gradient-based and incremental methods for learning them.
